study_identification.title: Beyond homogeneity: charting the landscape of heterogeneity in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric electroencephalography

study_characteristics.study_objective: To combine high-density EEG with normative modeling to quantify electrophysiological heterogeneity in spectral power and functional connectivity among patients with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders (ADHD, ASD, anxiety, learning disorder), and to explore whether deviation-based markers can enhance comparative analysis and correlate with clinical assessments.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Fully automated multi-stage pipeline: bandpass filter 1–100 Hz; downsample to 200 Hz; PyPREP (RANSAC-based bad channel detection and interpolation); common average re-referencing; ICA with ICLabel (automated rejection of eye blink components); second bandpass filter 1–45 Hz; epoch segmentation (10-second epochs); Autoreject (automated detection and cleaning/rejection of bad epochs); eLORETA source reconstruction; BEM head model (age-specific MRI template); Desikan-Killiany atlas (68 ROIs); AEC functional connectivity with orthogonalization for leakage correction; MNE-Python; BrainNet Viewer; NBS
preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The Methods section provides a detailed, step-by-step description of the preprocessing pipeline including software packages, filtering parameters, bad channel/epoch detection methods, source reconstruction, and connectivity estimation. Variations for specific datasets (e.g., ABCCT without Autoreject, femaleASD pre-segmented) are also noted.
preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: The EEG preprocessing and artifact removal pipeline is executed through a multi-stage, fully automated algorithm. Initially, EEG signals undergo bandpass filtering between 1 and 100 Hz, focusing on the relevant frequency range for subsequent analysis. Signals were downsampled to 200 Hz. Bad EEG channels are identified using the pyprep algorithm, which employs a RANSAC-based approach, and these channels are subsequently interpolated using information from neighboring electrodes [47, 48]. ... Then, re-referencing is performed using the common average reference method to minimize common noise across electrodes. Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is then applied, and the IClabel algorithm automatically identifies and rejects components related to eye blinks [49]. A second bandpass filter narrows the frequency range to 1-45 Hz, refining the data further. The EEG signals are segmented into 10-second epochs based on experimental paradigms (e.g., eyes-open and eyes-closed). The Autoreject toolbox [50] is utilized for the detection and cleaning/rejection of bad epochs, ensuring the removal of artifacts or irregularities. ... cortical sources are computed using the exact low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (eLORETA) which aims to reconstruct the cortical activity from EEG data with correct localization [51]. ... Age-specific head models of the three layers (brain, skull, and scalp) were built using an MRI template of young children (4-18 y) [52]. We used the Boundary Element Method (BEM) provided by the MNE Python package. ... Then, to streamline the complexity of the cortical sources, we downsampled them to 68 representative sources by averaging the sources within each region as defined by the Desikan-Killiany atlas [53]. Subsequently, we computed functional connectivity between pairwise regions of interest, using the amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) method, defined as the Pearson correlation between signals' envelopes derived from the Hilbert transform [36, 37]. Zero-lag signal overlaps caused by spatial leakage were removed using a pairwise orthogonalization approach before connectivity computation [38].

quality_checking_detail.supporting_text: Bad EEG channels are identified using the pyprep algorithm, which employs a RANSAC-based approach, and these channels are subsequently interpolated using information from neighboring electrodes [47, 48]. RANSAC works by randomly selecting a small group of EEG channels, estimating a model based on these channels, and then identifying channels that deviate from the model as potential outliers or bad channels. This process is repeated to find a model that best fits the majority of channels while disregarding outliers. ... Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is then applied, and the IClabel algorithm automatically identifies and rejects components related to eye blinks [49]. ... The Autoreject toolbox [50] is utilized for the detection and cleaning/rejection of bad epochs, ensuring the removal of artifacts or irregularities. All EEG datasets underwent the preprocessing steps described above, except when certain procedures were deemed infeasible. Notably, the Autoreject step was excluded from the preprocessing of the ABCCT dataset. The femaleASD dataset had already been preprocessed and segmented into 2-second epochs. Therefore, further preprocessing for this dataset was confined solely to downsampling and re-referencing. ... Electrode impedance checks were performed before recording, and values were maintained below 40 kΩ [HBN]. ... electrode impedance was assessed before each recording, ensuring it remained below 100 kΩ [ABCCT]. ... The impedance of each electrode is checked prior to recording to ensure good contact and is kept below 10 kΩ [LausanneASD].

modeling_method.answer: GAMLSS (Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape)
modeling_method.reason: The paper explicitly states that GAMLSS was used for normative modeling of both spectral power and functional connectivity features. GAMLSS is described as a semi-parametric regression framework allowing modeling of distribution parameters (location, scale, shape) as functions of covariates.
modeling_method.supporting_text: For each feature, we split our reference population (HC) into training and test sets, and trained a Generalized Additive Model for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS) on the training set. For the spectral features, a GAMLSS was fitted to the relative power (Welch's method) of each channel and each frequency band. ... A GAMLSS was fitted to the connectivity values at each connection and each frequency band. ... Normative Modeling (NM) seeks to establish a standard or normative relationship between a response variable (behavioral, demographic, or clinical variables) and at least one covariate (a quantitative biological measure, e.g. age, sex). In this context, Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS) [54], are semi-parametric regression models. In these models, the response variable is presumed to follow a specific distribution, wherein the parameters of this distribution can be linked to a set of explanatory variables via linear or nonlinear predictor functions, providing a flexible framework to capture complex relationships.

Residual plots: To assess the performance of our models, as recommended by Stasinopoulos et al. [55] we inspected their Q-Q plots. A good model is characterized by the presence of randomly scattered residuals around the horizontal zero line. Additionally, the kernel density estimate of the residuals should approximately follow a normal distribution, and an ideal Q-Q plot should exhibit linearity [55]. Upon reviewing our models, it appears that they demonstrate satisfactory fit and quality, Fig. S15, S16 in Supplementary Materials. Bootstrap analysis: The robustness and reliability of our model were assessed using bootstrap analysis. The original training set was resampled 1000 times with replacement, with the model being retrained on each of these resampled datasets. A distribution profile for the predicted median was constructed, capturing the inherent variability and stability of our model's performance. To offer a quantifiable measure of reliability, the 95% confidence intervals were calculated from the distribution profiles, Fig. S17, S18 in Supplementary Materials.

deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores (normalized quantile residuals, RQR); extreme deviation threshold |z| > 2; spatial overlap maps (percentage of subjects with extreme deviation at each channel/connection among those with at least one extreme deviation); global deviation score (average of extreme z-scores per subject) for clinical correlation; group-based permutation tests (n=5000) with FDR correction for comparing overlap maps; Network-Based Statistics (NBS) with permutation (n=5000) comparing z-score matrices vs original features.
deviation_metric.reason: The Methods section provides detailed description of deviation metrics: z-scores computed via modified quantile residual approach from GAMLSS, threshold for extreme deviation defined as |z| > 2, spatial overlap quantified as percentage of subjects showing extreme deviation at each location, global deviation score defined as average z-score of extremely deviated channels/connections, and statistical testing via permutation-based group comparisons and NBS.
deviation_metric.supporting_text: Subsequently, subjects with ASD, ADHD, ANX, and LD, along with an HC(test) group were projected on these models to calculate their deviation scores (z-scores, z). These deviations can be negative (lower than normative values) or positive (higher than normative values), Fig. 2a1, b1. Extreme deviations were defined as |z| > 2 [22, 24, 26-31], Fig. 2a2, b2. ... The z-scores, or deviation scores, are derived using a modified function from the gamlss library. They are computed as the inverse normal cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the model's fitted CDF, a method known as randomized quantile residuals (RQRs). According to Stasinopoulos et al. [55], when the model is properly trained, RQRs are equivalent to z-scores. An extreme deviation is defined as |z-score| > 2. Consequently, we derived positive and negative extreme deviation maps for z-scores > 2 and < -2, respectively. We then computed the number of subjects exhibiting at least one extreme deviation, as well as the number of extreme deviations per subject. Additionally, for each channel/connection, we assessed the percentage of subjects exhibiting extreme deviation at that location among those with at least one extreme deviation, leading to an overlap map of the extreme deviation in each group. ... We used group-based permutation tests to evaluate group differences in channel/connectivity-level overlap [22]. These tests involved shuffling cases and control labels of the individual-specific deviation maps. ... repeated 5,000 times ... two-tailed FDR correction (p < 0.05). ... Network-based statistical comparison and clinical associations of deviation scores. ... Using a network-based statistics -NBS- approach (permutation test, n = 5000) [39], we compared the clinical groups to the HC(test) using either the original functional connectivity matrices (the original features) or the deviation score (z-scores) matrices. Second, we explored the potential of NM to provide a framework for generating subject-specific markers that may correlate with clinical assessments of patients. For this purpose, we calculated a global deviation score for each subject, defined as the average z-score values of the extremely deviated channels/connections. This score was then correlated with the patients' clinical assessments (total ADOS scores -a standard clinical assessment in ASD-).

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Network-Based Statistics (NBS) permutation test (n=5000, FDR-corrected) comparing clinical groups to HC(test) using z-score matrices vs original functional connectivity matrices to identify significant network differences; Spearman correlation between global deviation scores (average z of extreme deviations in spectral/connectivity) and total ADOS scores in ASD patients; group-based permutation tests (n=5000, FDR-corrected) comparing channel/connection-level overlap maps between clinical groups and HC(test).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: EEG spectral power and functional connectivity deviations from normative models are highly heterogeneous across patients with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders; spatial overlap of deviations across patients is low (≤40% for spectral, ≤24% for connectivity); deviation-based features enhance group-level comparative analysis and correlate with clinical assessments (ADOS), supporting precision psychiatry approaches.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Across 1674 patients (ADHD, ASD, anxiety, learning disorder) and 560 healthy controls (448 training, 112 test), normative modeling revealed that patient deviations from population norms were highly heterogeneous and frequency-dependent. Spatial overlap of extreme deviations (|z| > 2) among patients with at least one deviation did not exceed 40% for spectral power (channel level) and 24% for functional connectivity (network level). For example, overlap in spectral features reached 40% in LD gamma band and 31% in ADHD delta band; connectivity overlap peaked at 24% in LD beta band and 23% in HC(test) alpha band. Traditional functional connectivity features showed no significant differences between HC and clinical groups using NBS, but z-score matrices revealed significant network differences (e.g., ASD vs HC: alpha p=0.0002 with 91 edges, beta p=0.007 with 12 edges; ADHD vs HC: delta p<0.0001 with 94 edges). Global deviation scores (average z-score of extreme deviations) correlated significantly with ADOS total scores in ASD (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.2, p<0.05), with positive deviations increasing and negative deviations decreasing with higher ADOS scores. These findings suggest that individual-level deviation patterns are highly patient-specific and that normative modeling can identify subject-specific markers associated with clinical severity.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Sample size (n=2234) is large for EEG but smaller than typical MRI studies and not population-representative; unbalanced dataset composition with HBN contributing 1539/2234 subjects, potentially biasing results; generalizability limited to 128-channel EEG systems (five datasets all used 128-channel EGI Geodesic HydroCel); cross-sectional design precludes assessment of within-subject variability and developmental trajectories; restricted age range (5–18 years) may contribute to observed heterogeneity due to varying developmental stages; comorbidity among clinical groups introduces complexity (Table S1 shows many patients with multiple diagnoses); potential medication effects not fully controlled (HBN allowed stimulant use on study days if unable/unwilling to stop); feature selection limited to spectral power and connectivity (other features like alpha peak frequency not explored); GAMLSS per-feature modeling (separate models for each channel/connection/band) increases complexity and does not capture multivariate dependencies; lack of multi-response GAMLSS capability limits holistic subject-level deviation representation.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Deviation scores can serve as inputs for downstream analyses (group comparisons, classification, prediction) and may outperform raw features; subject-specific global deviation scores correlate with clinical assessments (ADOS), representing a step toward precision psychiatry via EEG; high heterogeneity challenges group-level biomarker development and supports need for individualized approaches; future work should explore other EEG features (e.g., alpha peak frequency for ADHD subtyping), combine modalities (EEG+MRI), develop multi-response GAMLSS, and incorporate longitudinal data; code available at https://github.com/MINDIG-1/NM-Psy.git.

general_notes.general_notes: This is the first study to systematically apply normative modeling to high-density EEG (HD-EEG) spectral power and functional connectivity in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. The study analyzed resting-state 128-channel EEG from five aggregated datasets (HBN, MIPDB, ABCCT, femaleASD, LausanneASD) spanning ages 5–18 years. Connectivity was computed in source space (eLORETA) between 68 Desikan-Killiany ROIs using amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) with orthogonalization to mitigate leakage. Spectral features were computed via Welch's PSD method and expressed as relative band power (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma). GAMLSS models were trained separately for each channel (124 channels after QC) and each connection (68×67/2 = 2278 unique ROI pairs) across five frequency bands, yielding thousands of individual models. Distribution families (e.g., SEP2, SEP4, GB2, BCPE, ST3, exGAUS) were empirically selected by BIC per feature (Table S4). Age was modeled via fractional polynomials (fp); site/sex included as fixed factors where selected by BIC (Tables S5–S6). Residual diagnostics (Q-Q plots, Figs. S15–S16) and bootstrap analyses (1000 iterations, 95% CIs, Figs. S17–S18) confirmed model fit and stability. Held-out HC(test) and clinical groups were projected to compute z-scores (RQR); extreme deviations defined as |z| > 2. Overlap maps quantified spatial consistency of deviations; group-based permutation tests (n=5000, FDR-corrected) compared clinical vs HC overlap. NBS analyses (n=5000 permutations) compared z-score vs raw connectivity matrices. Global deviation scores (average z of extremes) correlated with ADOS in ASD. Exploratory analyses controlled for sex (Figs. S2–S11, Tables S2–S3), IQ (Figs. S12–S14), and comorbidity (single-diagnosis subset analysis confirming low overlap). Supplementary tables (S7–S18) report detailed heterogeneity metrics (percentage with ≥1 extreme deviation, median/range of extreme counts, max overlap values per band/group). The study demonstrates that EEG deviations are highly individualized and frequency-dependent, challenging group-level case-control paradigms and supporting precision psychiatry frameworks. Full dataset details (sample sizes, demographics, inclusion/exclusion criteria, EEG acquisition protocols) provided in Supplementary Methods for each of the five datasets. Ethics approvals obtained from Chesapeake IRB, Yale IRB, and Swiss CER-VD.
